jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: Lawn Portfolio
jokes.joke: I’m a stock market trader, so I manage my backyard like a portfolio. I bought grass high, watched it go brown, then doubled down because I believed in the fundamentals. My neighbor said, “Why don’t you just water it?” I said, “Absolutely not. I’ve already diversified into weeds.”

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Hedge Fund Tomatoes
jokes.joke: My brother-in-law is a stock market trader. He says my backyard garden is a terrible investment. Fair. I put in four hundred dollars of soil, fencing, and seeds, and I got six tomatoes. That's sixty-seven dollars a tomato. But I told him, 'Look, it's a growth stock.' He said, 'Is it growing?' I said, 'No, but it's very emotionally volatile. Yesterday a squirrel took a thirty percent haircut.'

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Garden Speculation
jokes.joke: I used to be a stock market trader, which ruined my ability to just enjoy a backyard garden. I don't plant vegetables; I speculate on commodities. This spring I went long on heirloom tomatoes. By July, the aphids hit, the yield plummeted, and I panicked. I completely liquidated the cucumbers to cover my margins, and my wife caught me screaming at a squirrel for insider trading at the bird feeder.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Backyard Day Trader
jokes.joke: I became a stock market trader working from my backyard. Every morning I drag a lawn chair under the tree, open the laptop, and start barking orders at the charts. I yell buy and the squirrels freeze. I yell sell and the dog runs inside. One day a bird landed on the keyboard and I market-bought a thousand shares of whatever was under the cursor. Turns out it was a birdseed company. Finally, a trade the whole backyard could get behind.

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Free-Range Portfolio
jokes.joke: I live next to a guy who treats his backyard chickens like a stock portfolio. Every morning he gives me a market update: one hen is underperforming, another has strong egg fundamentals. Last week he tried to sell me a dozen eggs and called it an IPO: an Initial Poultry Offering.

scores.comment: Strong escalation from investment math to market language; the squirrel haircut is a clean, concrete final image.
Best-developed premise in the batch, with natural escalation and a strong closing image in the squirrel insider-trading accusation.
Clear and well structured, but the accidental birdseed trade feels engineered toward the pun rather than genuinely surprising.
Concise and understandable, but the joke depends heavily on the predictable Initial Poultry Offering pun, limiting surprise.
Compact premise with a decent final turn ('diversified into weeds'). The portfolio-as-lawn conceit is familiar, but the ending lands cleanly.
Trading jargon applied to gardening is a predictable route. The squirrel insider-trading line is the best beat, but the setup runs long and the ending is overloaded.

Fun visual premise and the bird-on-keyboard trade is a good turn. The closer ('a trade the whole backyard could get behind') is a soft, explanatory ending that undercuts the snap, and the piece runs long.

Clean, economical, and clearly structured, but the 'Initial Poultry Offering' pun is the kind of wordplay ending that earns a groan more than a laugh. Predictable once the chicken portfolio is set up.
Clean stage rhythm and a solid premise. 'Diversified into weeds' is a competent, if slightly predictable, payoff.
Excellent stand-up cadence. The $67 tomato math is highly relatable, and the '30% haircut' squirrel line perfectly bridges both concepts for a strong laugh.
Leans too heavily into cartoonish whimsy. The bird buying birdseed stock feels like a contrived story rather than grounded stand-up.
Relies entirely on a dad-joke pun (IPO/Poultry). The setup merely exists to deliver the wordplay rather than an insightful comic idea.
Clean analogy but predictable; weeds line is mild and expected.
Solid cost-per-tomato setup; squirrel haircut lands as a real mild turn.
Good escalation from speculation to liquidation; squirrel insider-trading close carries a genuine laugh.
Pun-dependent IPO payoff feels thin and familiar; premise is clear but forgettable.
Clear premise and solid analogy; weeds as diversification is a mild but predictable payoff.
Good escalation from bad investment to emotional volatility; squirrel haircut line adds a stronger turn.
Nicely sustained trader-garden framing; insider trading by a squirrel is a playful, memorable finish.
Well-structured story with a clean callback to the backyard; birdseed-company reveal lands effectively.
